title: Camp 3 close: the practice is yours
hook: sixty days of tools; next, a poet and an emperor

segments.voice: Yesterday, the missed day and the restart without a speech. Your line was just start again. Is it written at the bottom of your list? Day one hundred fifty-six.

Sixty days ago, this camp started with a promise in four words: I can do this. Not I understand this, or I've read about this. Do. Back then, practice might have sounded like something other people did: monks, athletes, people with more time. Look at what you've done since. You've watched ten breaths and sighed on purpose. You've previewed mornings and reviewed evenings. You've sorted worries into mine and not mine, counted good things, looked down from a mile up, and remembered you will die. You've walked, scanned, slept, served, hidden your phone and watched the sun go. Today, the last day of the camp, we put it together. Today is camp three close.
screen: `SIXTY DAYS AGO: I CAN DO THIS.` → `LOOK WHAT YOU'VE DONE.` → `CAMP THREE CLOSE.`

segments.voice: Here's the whole camp, in order. Week one: breath, from just watching to box breathing. Week two: bookends, Marcus's morning preview and Seneca's evening review. Week three: the dichotomy of control, Epictetus's two columns. Week four: gratitude, three good things and grace before meals. Week five: the view from above, the pale blue dot, memento mori and the Buddha's five remembrances. Week six: walking, the body scan and sleep. Week seven: service, one act a week. Week eight: the digital sabbath, borrowed with respect from Shabbat. Week nine: sunset as a ritual. And this last week: your five, their smallest versions, and starting again. The Stoics had a word for all this: askesis, training, the way an athlete trains. Epictetus taught that philosophy isn't only for reading; it's exercise, done daily, in small reps. Dictionaries trace the English word ascetic to the same Greek root, but the older sense is simpler: practice. And that's what this camp was. Not beliefs to adopt. Nobody on this path has told you what to believe. Tools, borrowed carefully from traditions and from science, each named, each left in its own home. What you do with them is yours. Now the path turns. The next camp is about a text, read slowly: two books, side by side. One by a thirteenth-century Persian poet, a Muslim scholar named Jalal al-Din Rumi. One by a second-century Roman emperor, writing private notes to himself: Marcus Aurelius, whom you've already met. Two voices, never merged.
screen: `NINE WEEKS OF TOOLS.` · `ASKESIS: TRAINING.` · `TOOLS, NOT BELIEFS.` · `NEXT: A POET AND AN EMPEROR.` · then, large: `I CAN DO THIS.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: do your whole routine once, in its smallest form. Settle. For your first practice, one breath's worth. Then the second. Then the third, the fourth, the fifth. If one is a walk or a sunset, picture it for a breath. When you've done all five, rest, and feel it: that was your whole routine, and it fit inside two minutes. Say inside: I can do this. The bell holds the time.
Camp three close. Sixty days of practices, from breath to sunset, gathered into a routine that's yours. Today's word.
Your line: I can do this. Today, do your whole routine once, at full size if you can, smallest size if you can't. Both count. Tomorrow, two books. Day one hundred fifty-six.

screen: `DAY 156 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: TWO BOOKS FOR ONE CAMP.`

howItsDone: People who keep a personal spiritual practice outside a single tradition often settle on a short daily routine of a few practices, such as breath, a morning intention, an evening review and a walk, and adjust it over time.

match.prompt: which week, which practice — tap the pairs.

fork.setup: the camp is over. you have five practices and their smallest versions. what now?
options: put the list away; the camp is done.
fork.reveal: keep doing them, your way. askesis means training, and training is daily, in small reps.

original.note: Greek, askesis: training, exercise. the Stoics used it for daily practice; English 'ascetic' comes from it.

trapdoor: what you thought: a spiritual practice means giving things up.
what it means: practice means training, daily and small, with tools that fit your life.
what a scholar hears: askesis, athletic training before it meant self-denial; Epictetus's discourse 'On Training' (Discourses 3.12).
